articles.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
articles.standfirst: Networks of plumbers and electricians are scamming people on a large scale, the BBC reveals.
paragraphs: Nessar Khawaja told almost 70,000 social media followers his network makes money from "desperate" customers
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.
"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.
The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.
The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.
In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".
In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.
"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.
One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.
After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".
Clive was billed £9,153 by a suspected rogue trader for fitting an outdoor socket in his garden
Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.
The impact can be devastating.
Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.
He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.
An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.
Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.
He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.
Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.
"I was shocked," said Clive.
He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.
He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.
Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.
"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.
"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."
While the BBC has not seen evidence that Khawaja controls or runs this company, it has established the following:
Companies House places Chriss Electrician Ltd at an address in Ilford
Khawaja appears as the listed director of two dissolved companies inside that same building, one inside the very same flat
Khawaja's company First Choice Maintenance 24/7 Limited was registered 22 days before Chriss Electrician Ltd was incorporated and registered at the same flat as its address.
The BBC contacted Chriss Electrician Ltd for comment but it has not responded.
Khawaja denied having any connection with Chriss Electrician Ltd.
Clive was refunded by his bank after it was contacted by the BBC. The bank said it had done so as a "gesture of goodwill".
Like Clive, another man, who the BBC has named as Tom, felt he had no choice but to settle the bill when he mistakenly called a rogue trader to his property in Essex after finding a leak.
He says he was initially quoted £49 over the phone after calling a listing at the top of Google purporting to be an established business.
But on arrival, the plumber increased the call-out fee to £250 and the costs kept on climbing.

"He charged us for the first load of repairs, and then the second load with the water cylinder. Basically, he was running my taps constantly saying, 'Look, it's coming out this hot', which caused me to panic."
By the end, the plumber presented a bill for £6,237.60.
"I noticed afterwards that the invoice said Ibby & Co. Ltd. That was when alarm bells started ringing because I had never heard of that company. It wasn't the company I called out, essentially."
Tom called another plumber to get a second opinion and was told the work that was completed should have cost no more than £1,000.

When Tom called the company to complain, he received threats from an unknown man. The call was recorded and the BBC heard threats including: "We'll show up at your house. And we're gonna be sleeping there for months."
Ibrahim Nazir, the plumber who came to Tom's property and the listed director of Ibby and Co Ltd, has been contacted by the BBC for comment but has not responded.
Sources close to Khawaja place Nazir inside the same network.
Khawaja said he did not know anything about the job involving Tom and stated Nazir was not in his employ.
Monetising vulnerability and desperation is key to the rogue trader business model, insiders say.
One insider forwarded the BBC a script being circulated by a different rogue trader network recruiting young men for commission-based work.
The document tells recruits to hike prices if children or pets are trapped inside and even instructs them to fake picking a lock for seven minutes before drilling it.
Lee, not his real name, spent a year working for Khawaja as a plumber until, he says, his conscience got the better of him.
"It got a bit too much for me," he said. "I didn't like scamming people. So, I left.
"I've worked for London's biggest plumbing company and, no word of a lie, this lot have more jobs. They're giants."
Rather than relying on solid reputations and recommendation, rogue traders rely on search engine traffic.
They either pay to get their details at the top of Google, which means they are seen first, or they mimic the names of reputable companies by making tiny changes to the business name.
Reached by the BBC's undercover journalist posing as a plumber seeking to work with them, one of Khawaja's associates said: "We're a lead company. We'll send you jobs, and then you go to the jobs.
"We sort the jobs through online advertisement. Usually we'll try and get emergencies so we can charge more. You make up the pricing."
The associate told the undercover reporter they had to charge in the region of £400 for every job, regardless of what work was actually needed.
Both Clive and Tom reported what happened to the Metropolitan Police and Essex Police.
Khawaja said he was not a party to the phone call with the undercover journalist and could not comment on its contents.
He said the alleged statements did not reflect how he operates.
He separately told the BBC in the recorded phone call: "You guys should know I am an entertainer and you guys are taking it out of context."
"I am clearly joking and I'm entertaining and I am engaging with the comments, it is not literal," he added.
He said the right of reply sent to him by the BBC contained "false information which has nothing to do with me".
TikTok said its community guidelines were "clear" and did not "allow any attempts to scam, trick or defraud people".
The firm said in the three months up to June 2026, it had removed 99.2% of content found to be in breach of its "policies on fraud and scams... before it was reported to us".

The BBC put questions to Google including why rogue traders were able to advertise on its platform. It did not answer specific questions, but a Google spokesperson said: "We have strict ads policies that govern the types of ads and advertisers we allow on our platforms.
"Keeping our users and partners safe is our top priority and we invest heavily in the enforcement of our policies.
"We have a team of thousands working around the clock to create and enforce our policies at scale."

articles.title: The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
articles.standfirst: RSPCA hands out food, vet vouchers, cat litter and toys to pet owners struggling with bills.
paragraphs: John Paul Feely has five pets and used the pet food bank to help relieve the pressure of growing bills
At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets.
The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food.
Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions.
John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends £35 a month on them.
"At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says.
Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.
A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Feely lives with his partner and explains that they are already making tough decisions about "turning the lights out and not putting the heating on".
He is able to take home food supplies and a dog chew toy.
Angela Gillot says the pop-up pet food bank is a big help
As food bank volunteers offer tea and coffee to those waiting in the queue, Angela Gillot accepts a small dog jacket from the RSPCA stall with a smile.
She explains with a tear in her eye that since becoming unemployed she has felt the pinch of rising bills.
The RSPCA estimates that the cost of keeping a small dog like a Jack Russell could be up to £209 a month.
Energy costs going up next year "will affect everything," Gillot admits, as she describes how she and her dog huddle up under a blanket to keep warm.
"We do love these pets. We're a pet-loving nation aren't we? But it's getting harder.
"When I got my dogs I was working, so I try my best, but the price of food, especially what's of quality, I just really can't afford it.
"It's not often you go to these places and they think about your pets," the 58-year-old says.
Tricia Watts, the upbeat assistant manger at Burngreave Foodbank, is enthusiastic about the support from the RSPCA.
She explains that while the food bank works with people in food poverty, it cannot always help people with animal care as it relies on donations.
She has seen demand increase, and donations fall, in the seven years she has worked at the food bank.
"I think pets are so important to people. If people are going through hard times, they're still important and they don't want to lose them."
Growing bills are of particular concern to exotic animal owners as many birds, reptiles and fish must be kept in carefully maintained conditions that are often energy-intensive.
Carl Chandler runs Sustainable Aquatics in Rotherham. He says rising energy prices have had a "gigantic" impact on his business.
Chandler caveats that fish are one of the most wallet-friendly pets.
"To run a tropical fish tank you're looking less than a cup of coffee a week."
Other species, however, require specialist equipment to replicate their natural habitats.
"Reptiles, frogs and amphibians are incredibly expensive to heat because you need UV bulbs and to keep the right humidity."
Katie Hetherington, left, and Lucy Sollner, right, work with the RSPCA to support pet owners
Back in Burngreave, the pop-up event has managed to give away as much as 50kg of food, the equivalent of more than 100 tins, to pet owners in need.
Sometimes, of course, owners find the challenge simply too much, and give their pets up for rehoming.
"We've seen heartbreaking examples across the country of people leaving notes with animals saying they just can't afford them any more," Chris O'Brien, a spokesperson for the RSPCA, says.
"The cost of giving crisis has put new levels of pressure on us in terms of animals coming in quicker than we can rehome them.
"As these cost of living bombshells keep coming, unfortunately it's going to be a continued difficult time for animal owners across the region."

articles.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
articles.standfirst: Why is Poundland closing down, and what will happen to staff and suppliers?
paragraphs: Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.
The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.
This is the question that is most difficult to answer.
Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.
Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.
Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.
But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.
A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.
That depends on who you ask.
When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.
Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.
The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.
However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.
A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".
"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."
Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.
Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.
Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.
The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.
This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.
If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.
In the short term, yes.
From 26 November you will not get a refund for goods if you change your mind about the purchase. If the item is faulty you will still get a refund.
The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers.
This meant that stock was running low at Poundland.
But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term.
If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it.
That depends on what happens next.
Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.
But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.
As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.
Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

articles.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
articles.standfirst: The changes could see drivers over 70 stripped of licences if they do not meet standards.
paragraphs: Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.
Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.
Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.
To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.
The change follows a consultation which launched early last year, set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.
Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".
But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.
The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail.
The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive.
The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous.
A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue.
"One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years.
The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over.
A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents.
"Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this.
"We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about."

articles.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
articles.standfirst: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
paragraphs: SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.

It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".

It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".

Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."
This video can not be played
The BBC visited Arizona before the US midterm elections to understand America's data-centre boom

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title: Learning from the DevoLab: How can mayors use their powers to deliver ‘good growth’?
articles.standfirst:
Learning from the DevoLab: How can mayors use their powers to deliver ‘good growth’? melissa.ittoo Thu, 26/11/2026 - 14:02 19 Case study Harriet Shaw Megan Isaac Akash Paun Institute for Government Yes Devolution Local government Health Welfare Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government IfG DevoLab
Learning from the DevoLab: How can mayors use their powers to deliver ‘good growth’?
No Eight lessons for how devolved powers can be best used in practice.

Summary 

The Burnham government has made devolution central to its plans for “good growth in every postcode”. It argues that delivering that growth will require “a fundamental rewiring of the way our country works”.1 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 11 August 2026, retrieved 11 August
2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-
statement-html  To achieve this, it has committed to putting “the most important powers to drive local growth in the hands of local leaders”, announcing further devolution of key responsibilities, including 16–19 technical skills, employment support, and funding for affordable housing, alongside new fiscal powers that will allow mayors to retain a share of income tax from 2028.2 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 11 August 2026, retrieved 11 August
2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html  

Mayors will be expected to use these powers, alongside their existing responsibilities for transport, housing, adult skills, investment and economic development, to deliver good growth. At the same time, the government has committed to establishing strategic authorities across the country by the end of 2028.3 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 11 August 2026, retrieved 11 August
2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html  

The government describes its push for “good growth” as an approach in which “economic progress goes hand in hand with social progress underpinned by democratic accountability.”4 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 11 August 2026, retrieved 11 August
2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-
statement-html  This indicates that good growth will not be judged only by economic outcomes but also by its wider social impact. 

This term and approach stems from Burnham’s experience as mayor of Greater Manchester, which launched a Good Growth Fund in 2025 to “pioneer a new model of economic growth”.5 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, ‘Mayor Andy Burnham unveils plan to pioneer new model of economic growth with £1bn good growth fund’, 19 November 2025, retrieved 1 October 2026, www.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/news/mayor-andy-burnham-unveils-plan-to-pioneer-a-new-model-of-economic-growth-with-1bn-gm-good-growth-fund-and-pipel…  The fund aims to drive growth that is shared across the city region and leaves “no one or no place” behind.6 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, ‘Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund’, no date, retrieved 1 October 2026, www.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/what-we-do/economy/greater-manchester-good-growth-fund  It uses public investment to attract private capital and to direct capital to housing, employment and regeneration projects that support the wider policy goals of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA).7 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, ‘Report: Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund’, 28 November 2025, retrieved 1 October 2026, https://democracy.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/documents/s41037/5C%20Good%20Growth%20Fund%20CA%20Paper%2018.11.25.pdf  At the 2026 budget, the government announced £285m of capital funding to establish good growth funds in all mayoral areas and all areas progressing towards establishing a strategic authority.8 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Good Growth Funds: place selection and indicative allocations’, GOV.UK, 28 October 2026, retrieved 17 November 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/good-growth-funds-place-selection-and-indicative-allocations/good-growth-funds-place-selection-and-indicative-allo…

The IfG DevoLab

But devolving powers, though important, is only the first step to achieving good growth. The benefits of greater local control will depend on how effectively those powers are used in practice – and how effectively mayoral strategic authorities (MSAs) develop clear priorities, build regional partnerships and deliver for their residents. The challenge, then, is not simply to devolve power, but to make devolution work effectively.

Launched in July 2025, the IfG DevoLab aims to help achieve this. We have been exploring the policy innovations enabled by devolution, identifying what works and what places can learn from each other, holding events in Sheffield, Manchester, Leeds and Birmingham to experience the devolution programme first hand. Through 15 case studies spanning 10 mayoral regions, the series has examined how mayors and local leaders are using devolved powers to tackle some of their most pressing challenges. Links to the case studies are found throughout, and include:

  • reducing health inequalities
  • securing investment
  • improving transport connectivity
  • increasing the supply of affordable homes
  • developing a shared vision for regional growth.

As England enters a new phase of devolution, the experience of strategic authorities across different policy areas and places offers valuable insight into how devolved powers can be best used in practice. Drawing on those case studies, this paper identifies eight lessons that emerge consistently and that together provide practical guidance for mayors, local leaders and central government.

Key findings

  1. Mayors can provide visible and consistent leadership to maintain momentum and deliver long-term strategic priorities
  2. Mayors can convene local partners to develop innovative solutions to complex, cross-cutting challenges
  3. Mayors can spearhead the development of long-term growth strategies, founded on a robust evidence base, around which local parties can unite
  4. Mayors can enter into structured investment and regeneration partnerships with local authorities and other regional stakeholders to drive place-based growth 
  5. Mayors can join the dots and bring about coordinated intervention across transport, skills, housing and other drivers of good growth
  6. Mayors can allocate ‘just enough’ public investment to address viability challenges and catalyse private investment 
  7. Government can support mayors to succeed by accelerating progress towards funding simplification and fiscal devolution 
  8. Government can help build the capability and capacity of MSAs through direct funding, secondments and strategic partnerships

The lessons

1. Mayors can provide visible and consistent leadership to maintain momentum and deliver long-term strategic priorities 

Strong mayoral leadership can help regions deliver ambitious long-term projects that require sustained political support. By acting as a visible champion for flagship programmes, mayors can build public support, sustain momentum, and provide a clear point of accountability. They can also provide a strong, single voice for their regions, acting as a focal point for engagement with central government and investors. democracy.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/documents/s34954/GMCA%2020241129%20Delivering%20

2. Mayors can convene local partners to develop innovative solutions to complex, cross-cutting challenges 

Mayors can also use their convening powers to build partnerships around shared local priorities and address complex cross-organisational challenges, including in areas where they lack formal powers. To make progress on these challenges, mayors can develop pilot programmes to trial new approaches and test for proof of concept. 3. Mayors can spearhead the development of long-term growth strategies, founded on a robust evidence base, around which local parties can unite 

Mayors play an important role in defining a long-term strategic vision for their region, bringing local authorities, businesses and other partners together around shared priorities. Overarching regional strategies, such as the Greater Manchester Strategy and the West Yorkshire Plan, provide a framework for coordinating decision-making and investment across a place. These are supported by statutory plans, including local growth plans, spatial development strategies and local transport plans, which help translate ambition into action. 

As recommended by a previous Institute for Government report, effective strategies should be grounded in a strong evidence base, make clear choices about priorities and trade-offs, and build consensus among regional partners. Leaders do not need everyone to agree on everything but should establish a clear set of priorities around which partners can coordinate. 

For example, the East Midlands Combined County Authority (EMCCA) has developed the East Midlands Inclusive Growth Framework to provide a long-term, shared vision for inclusive growth in the region.1 East Midlands Combined County Authority, East Midlands Inclusive Growth Framework, October 2025, www.eastmidlands-cca.gov.uk/content/uploads/2025/10/2025-10-13-EM-Inclusive-Growth-Framework_FINAL.pdf  Developed through 12 months of research and engagement with partners, the framework defines inclusive growth as “a model of growth that values everyone’s contributions whilst also sharing out the benefits.”2 East Midlands Combined County Authority, East Midlands Inclusive Growth Framework, October
2025, www.eastmidlands-cca.gov.uk/content/uploads/2025/10/2025-10-13-EM-Inclusive-Growth-
Framework_FINAL.pdf  This concept has similarities with the government’s focus on ‘good growth’ and the importance of economic progress going “hand in hand with social progress”.3 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 11 August 2026, retrieved 11 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html  To achieve this, it sets out an overarching mission and six ambitions to guide investment, programme delivery and partnership working.

For a newer strategic authority with a relatively limited history of collaboration across the region, the framework provided an opportunity for EMCCA to not only address economic challenges but also to build relationships, develop a common sense of purpose and agree a set of shared priorities with partners across the region. 

Similarly, the Greater Manchester Strategy sets out a shared 10-year vision for the region, agreed by the 10 constituent local authorities in Greater Manchester.4 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, Greater Manchester Strategy, 2025, retrieved 21 August 2026,
https://togetherwearegm.co.uk/our-vision/greater-manchester-strategy/  The strategy guides specific programme priorities and investment: for example, the Sister innovation district is a key project within the Central Growth Cluster, one of the six growth locations identified in the strategy. Sister will help to deliver the strategy’s ambition for innovation-led regeneration and the creation of competitive sector clusters in advanced manufacturing, health innovation and digital technologies. 

The project also aims to support Greater Manchester’s overarching ambition of delivering good growth across the region, with Sister providing “opportunities for jobs, amenities and green space… it’s not just advanced manufacturing”.5 Edwards R, Presentation at ‘IfG DevoLab #2: How can mayors and strategic authorities secure investment into regional economies?’, Institute for Government event, 20 October 2025, retrieved 23 October 2026, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/event/devolab-2-mayors-strategic-authorities-secure-investment  

Shared goals developed at a local level can also play an important role in building consensus and coordinating action on growth ambitions. For example, the Sheffield City Goals were developed collaboratively by stakeholders from across the city to establish a shared set of 18 goals for Sheffield through to 2035. To support delivery, Sheffield City Council is also undertaking a series of neighbourhood conversations with residents to better understand local identities and ensure decisions are taken and services are delivered at the right level and in the right places. During the development of the Sheffield City Goals, the council engaged South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority and ensured the goals aligned with the regions broader strategic priorities especially in areas such as transport, skills, housing and economic development, where many of the key policy levers sit at the regional level.

4. Mayors can enter into structured investment and regeneration partnerships with local authorities and other regional stakeholders to drive place-based growth 

Mayors hold responsibilities across a range of policy areas that shape local economic performance, but they cannot deliver growth alone. Achieving mayoral priorities and delivering good growth requires partnerships with various stakeholders, including local authorities, delivery partners and central government. Mayors can do this by acting as system leaders, convening partners around shared priorities and coordinating collaborative working on regional projects. 

For MSAs, this requires recognition of where they can add value and where to bring partners in. For example, the Riverside Sunderland regeneration project is led by Sunderland City Council but supported by NEMSA. While the council leads on planning and regeneration, NEMSA has supported the project through revenue and investment funding and helping to align it with wider regional priorities.1 Riverside Sunderland, ‘£42m boost for Sunderland regeneration scheme’, 15 October 2024, retrieved 21 August 2026, https://riversidesunderland.com/ps42m-boost-sunderland-regeneration-scheme  For example, the project has been designated as part of NEMSA’s Creative Development Zone, with £300,000 investment from NEMSA, matched by Sunderland City Council, to unlock the project’s next phase of development.2 North East Mayoral Combined Authority, ‘New Mayoral Development Zone provides £600,000 boost to Sunderland’s future as a creative capital’, 10 December 2025, retrieved 21 August 2026, www.northeast-ca.gov.uk/news/culture-creative-tourism-and-sport/new-mayoral-development-zone-provides-600-000-boost-to-sunderland-s-future-as-a-creat…

5. Mayors can join the dots and bring about coordinated intervention across transport, skills, housing and other drivers of good growth

Mayors are well placed to lead this coordination and to align their powers and funding behind a shared vision for their region. 

For example, several mayors are developing integrated transport networks, recognising that improved transport connectivity can be an important driver of good growth. 6. Mayors can allocate ‘just enough’ public investment to address viability challenges and catalyse private investment 

Delivering good growth requires strategic investment in housing, transport and regeneration projects, which cannot be met through public funding alone. MSAs can play an important role in de-risking infrastructure projects and catalysing private investment. To achieve this, mayors can develop pipelines of priority projects and investment vehicles that can blend public and private finance to target investment towards regional priorities.

7. Government can support mayors to succeed by accelerating progress towards funding simplification and fiscal devolution 

Short-term, fragmented and ring-fenced funding can undermine strategic planning and make it harder for mayors to deliver on long-term priorities. Regions have shown the benefits that can arise from longer-term funding certainty. In Liverpool City Region, Merseyside’s Special Rail Grant settlement from the Department for Transport has given Merseytravel and the combined authority the sustained funding certainty required to take a strategic, long-term approach to improving the rail network. This has allowed for the local procurement of Class 777 trains, which it owns outright.1 Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, Long Term Rail Strategy, 2018, https://api.liverpoolcityregion-ca.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/LCRCA_RAIL_STRATEGY_MAY18.pdf  Ownership of the trains gives the city region greater control to shape investment, maintenance and service improvements around local priorities, rather than relying on decisions made by outside parties. 

West Yorkshire Mass Transit, a large-scale tram system planned to connect the region’s five core urban centres, will require significant capital investment, with the first phase estimated to cost between £2bn and £2.5bn.2 West Yorkshire Combined Authority, ‘West Yorkshire Mass Transit: progress update and further development funding release’, 25 July 2024, retrieved 18 August 2026, https://westyorkshire.moderngov.co.uk/mgConvert2PDF.aspx?ID=37589  Despite its completion date being pushed back several years due to an independent review, the government’s commitment of £2.1bn through the Transport for City Regions programme has been crucial for providing the first phase of the project with greater certainty and a sense of momentum.3 Department for Transport, ‘Transport for City Regions funding allocations’, 4 June 2025, retrieved 18 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/transport-for-city-regions-funding-allocations , 4 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 31 July 2026, retrieved 18 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html , 5 Blackburn R, ‘Delays for long-awaited Leeds mass transit opening, Tracy Brabin reveals’, Yorkshire Evening Post, 17 December 2025, retrieved 18 August 2026, www.yorkshireeveningpost.co.uk/news/politics/leeds-mass-transit-network-opening-delayed-until-late-2030s-5446915

Government should continue to build on the progress they have made with funding simplification to date. The introduction of integrated settlements for established MSAs was an important first step. By bringing multiple funding streams into a single flexible pot with multi-year certainty, integrated settlements have provided eligible mayors with greater freedom to allocate resources and have supported more effective long-term decision making. The government’s recent announcements that mayors will retain a share of business rates and income tax is a welcome further step, moving beyond funding flexibility and towards greater fiscal autonomy.6 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 31 July 2026, retrieved 18 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html

8. Government can help build the capability and capacity of MSAs through direct funding, secondments and strategic partnerships 

To make a success of their powers, and further powers coming down the line, mayors and strategic authorities need strong institutional capacity and delivery capability to coordinate programmes of investment. 

The government recognises that the success of devolution rests “on local institutions having the firepower and backing to use their powers effectively” and has committed to building up capacity in MSAs and local authorities.1 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the state – Cabinet statement’, GOV.UK, 31 July 2026, retrieved 18 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html  It can support capacity through long-term funding, secondments, strategic partnerships, sharing best practice and increased capacity funding. In August 2026, the government announced a package of measures to strengthen local capacity, including the secondment of high-performing civil servants into MSAs, with every MSA receiving between five and ten officials for periods of six to nine months, a new civil service fast stream pilot in Yorkshire and the Humber, and a digital devolution programme to build data and digital capability in MSAs.2 Prime Minister’s Office, 10 Downing Street, ‘Whitehall officials to be posted into mayors’ offices as PM
marks first month of No10 North’, GOV.UK, 21 August 2026, retrieved 27 August 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/whitehall-officials-to-be-posted-into-mayors-offices-as-pm-marks-first-month-of-no10-north  

Another way to build MSA capacity is through strategic partnerships with national delivery bodies. Housing projects require significant technical, financial and delivery expertise, which are often in short supply across the sector. To build capacity and support housing growth and regeneration, Homes England has agreed ‘strategic place partnerships’ with 10 MSAs. These partnerships align national housing and regeneration investments with the strategic priorities of elected mayors, providing an opportunity for Homes England to share technical expertise and delivery capacity with MSAs, while also helping Homes England to align housing investment with regional needs and priorities. 

For example, WCMA’s ‘strategic place partnership’ with Homes England commits both organisations to work collaboratively to accelerate housebuilding in the region, with a particular focus on remediating “difficult to deliver and stalled brownfield sites”, in line with the region’s ‘brownfield first’ approach.3 West Midlands Combined Authority and Homes England, West Midlands Strategic Place Partnership
Business Plan, 2025, https://governance.wmca.org.uk/documents/s15605/Enc.%202%20for%20West%20Midlands%20Strategic%20Place%20Partnership%20Update.pdf , 4 West Midlands Combined Authority, ‘Region’s ambitious target to build 215,000 new homes remains on
track’, 12 January 2024, retrieved 30 September 2026, www.wmca.org.uk/news/region-s-ambitious-target-to-build-215-000-new-homes-remains-on-track  Through the partnership, WMCA and Homes England are developing a pipeline of priority housing projects that require joint intervention from both partners.5 West Midlands Combined Authority, ‘Homes England and West Midlands Combined Authority launch
Strategic Place Partnership’, 15 March 2024, retrieved 21 August 2026, www.wmca.org.uk/news/homes-england-and-west-midlands-combined-authority-launch-strategic-place-partnership

MSA partnerships with Homes England also look set to develop further. In October 2026, Liverpool City Region became the first MSA to sign a Place Delivery Agreement with Homes England and the National Housing Bank.6 Homes England, ‘Liverpool City Region and Homes England sign first Place Delivery Agreement’. GOV.UK, 2 October 2026, retrieved 23 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/liverpool-city-region-and-homes-england-sign-first-place-delivery-agreement  The agreement establishes a dedicated joint delivery unit bringing together staff from all three organisations and is intended to move the relationship “from collaboration to co-delivery.”7 Homes England, ‘Liverpool City Region and Homes England sign first Place Delivery Agreement’. GOV.UK, 2 October 2026, retrieved 23 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/liverpool-city-region-and-homes-england-sign-first-place-delivery-agreement

Similar arrangements are emerging between MSAs and organisations such as the National Wealth Fund and Great British Railways (GBR), enabling MSAs to access specialist expertise and strengthen their delivery capability, while also helping these national bodies better understand and respond to local priorities. At our DevoLab event on transport connectivity, Richard Crabtree, head of mayoral partnerships at GBR, noted that through the Railways Bill, MSAs are being positioned as natural partners to GBR, with GBR able to support regions with expertise in railway delivery and mayors bringing their place-based knowledge.8 Crabtree R, Presentation at ‘IfG DevoLab #3: How devolution can improve transport connectivity’,
Institute for Government event, 6 November 2025, retrieved 23 October 2026, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/event/devolab-3-devolution-transport-connectivity
